name: Drometrizole trisiloxane

angle.text: Drometrizole trisiloxane (Mexoryl XL) is a photostable filter in L'Oreal-brand sunscreens and daily-wear skincare, often paired with ecamsule, used by people seeking everyday protection against skin aging. Evidence is formulation and regulatory data, not appearance trials.

summary: Photostable L'Oreal UVA/UVB sunscreen filter (Mexoryl XL), approved in the EU and elsewhere but not in the US.
note: Not an FDA-approved US sunscreen active; rare contact-allergy case reports.
currentQuick:
Drometrizole trisiloxane, sold as Mexoryl XL, is an organic UV filter that absorbs both UVB and UVA light. It is commonly paired with ecamsule (Mexoryl SX) in sunscreens.
It is approved in the EU, Canada, Australia and Japan but not in the United States. Evidence on it comes mainly from formulation and photoprotection studies of finished products.
How it works: It absorbs ultraviolet radiation, with peaks around 303 nm and 344 nm, and converts it to less harmful energy within the sunscreen film.
Risks and caveats: Case reports describe allergic contact dermatitis to it. It is not an approved US sunscreen active, so US availability depends on products using other filters.
deepLead:
Drometrizole trisiloxane (INCI name; sold by L'Oreal as Mexoryl XL, also called silatrizole) is a lipophilic benzotriazole-derived organic ultraviolet filter used in sunscreens and daily-wear skincare products . It is described as a broad-spectrum absorber with peaks near 303 nm (UVB) and 344 nm (UVA) and is frequently formulated together with ecamsule (Mexoryl SX) .
It is approved for sunscreens in the European Union, Canada, Australia, Japan and other countries but is not approved in the United States . In appearance-focused skincare it is mentioned in discussions of photoprotection against pigmentation and photoaging; published work is mostly formulation, photoprotection and contact-allergy research rather than trials of cosmetic outcomes.

name: Enzacamene

angle.text: Enzacamene (4-MBC) is an older camphor-derived UVB filter that appeared in sunscreens, where the aim was protecting skin from sun aging. It is now banned in EU cosmetics, so it mainly comes up in ingredient-checking discussions. Appearance outcomes were not studied for it specifically.

summary: Camphor-derived UVB sunscreen filter (4-MBC) now banned in EU cosmetics over endocrine-activity findings.
note: Banned in EU cosmetics (2024) and reportedly the UK and China; not FDA-approved.
currentQuick:
Enzacamene (4-MBC) is an organic UVB filter once used in sunscreens, especially in Europe. Regulators have since moved against it because of endocrine-activity research.
It is still permitted in some countries, such as Canada, while the EU has banned it in cosmetics and the US never approved it.
How it works: It absorbs UVB light and dissipates the energy partly through cis-trans isomerisation, though its photostability is described as limited.
Risks and caveats: Lab and animal studies reported estrogenic and thyroid effects, and human studies detected it in plasma, urine and milk. The EU SCCS found sufficient evidence of endocrine disruption in 2022.
deepLead:
Enzacamene (4-methylbenzylidene camphor, 4-MBC) is a camphor-derived organic UVB filter that has been used in sunscreens and SPF-labelled skincare . It has been the subject of endocrine-activity research, and it has been banned in cosmetics in the European Union (Regulation (EU) 2024/996), with further bans reported in the UK and China .
It remains permitted in some places, including Canada (up to 4%) and, per the source, Australia; it is not FDA-approved in the United States . It is discussed in sunscreen-ingredient communities mainly in the context of ingredient safety and regional availability.

name: Amiloxate

angle.text: Amiloxate is a cinnamate UVB filter found in EU sunscreens, used for general sun protection that helps skin stay even and youthful. Its appearance benefit is inferred from sunscreen-class evidence; beyond photoallergy case reports, little specific to it is studied.

summary: Cinnamate UVB sunscreen filter approved in the EU since 1997; photoallergy case reports exist and little else is studied.
note: Not an approved US OTC sunscreen active.
currentQuick:
Amiloxate is a cinnamate-type UVB filter used in some sunscreens, approved in the EU since 1997.
Published work on it is mostly analytical and environmental, plus case reports of photoallergic contact dermatitis.
How it works: It absorbs UVB radiation within the sunscreen film.
Risks and caveats: Photoallergic contact dermatitis has been reported. It is not an approved US OTC sunscreen active.
deepLead:
Amiloxate (isoamyl p-methoxycinnamate, isopentyl 4-methoxycinnamate, IMC) is a cinnamate ester used as a UVB filter in sunscreen products . It has been approved in the European Union since 1997; in the United States it has been under regulatory evaluation rather than listed as an approved sunscreen active .
Published literature on it consists mainly of analytical methods, environmental occurrence studies, and photoallergy reports.

name: Bisdisulizole disodium

angle.text: Bisdisulizole disodium (Neo Heliopan AP) is a water-soluble UVA filter in EU sunscreens, used in light textures that suit daily facial wear and protect against UVA-linked wrinkles and dark spots. Evidence is regulatory and formulation-based, not appearance trials.

summary: Water-soluble UVA sunscreen filter (Neo Heliopan AP), EU-approved since 2000 and not approved in the US.
note: Sparse published literature; not US-approved.
currentQuick:
Bisdisulizole disodium is a water-soluble UVA filter sold by Symrise as Neo Heliopan AP.
It is approved in the EU at up to 10% but not in the US. Few sources document it in detail.
How it works: It absorbs UVA radiation in the sunscreen formulation.
Risks and caveats: No safety information was found in the sources reviewed; it is not approved in the United States.
deepLead:
Bisdisulizole disodium (trade name Neo Heliopan AP, from Symrise; also abbreviated DPDT) is a water-soluble organic UVA filter used in sunscreens . It is a disodium salt with two sulfonated benzimidazole units on a phenylene core .
It has been approved in the European Union since 2000 at up to 10% in sunscreen formulations and is not approved in the United States .

name: Meradimate

angle.text: Meradimate is an older anthranilate UVA filter listed in US sunscreen rules, used to add some UVA coverage that helps protect skin from sun aging. It has been studied mostly for its photophysics rather than for appearance outcomes.

summary: Older US-listed anthranilate UVA sunscreen filter, studied mostly for its photophysics.
note: Lab findings only; no dedicated clinical trials found.
currentQuick:
Meradimate (menthyl anthranilate) is a UVA filter listed among the FDA's OTC sunscreen ingredients and used in some products alongside other filters.
Research on it is mainly photophysical and in vitro.
How it works: It absorbs UVA light and has been characterised as fluorescent, with studies mapping its excited-state behaviour.
Risks and caveats: Labels advise stopping use if rash occurs. Lab studies have examined cell effects and sperm-signalling interactions of UV filters; no clinical outcome data were found.
deepLead:
Meradimate (menthyl anthranilate) is an ester of anthranilic acid and menthol that acts as a UVA filter in sunscreens . It is one of the 17 ingredients the US FDA lists for over-the-counter sunscreen products . It should not be confused with methyl anthranilate .
Published research on it is mostly photophysical. A US label for a sports sunscreen lists it with octinoxate, octisalate and oxybenzone .

name: Padimate O

angle.text: Padimate O is an older PABA-derived UVB filter once common in sunscreens and lip products, used to protect skin from sun damage. It is rarely used now and appears mostly in ingredient history discussions; appearance outcomes were not studied for it specifically.

summary: Older PABA-derived UVB filter, now rarely used, with mixed lab data on photochemistry.
note: Lab studies on photomutagenicity and hormone-receptor activity; no dedicated clinical trials found.
currentQuick:
Padimate O is a PABA-derived oily UVB filter used in some sunscreens and lip products.
It is now less common, and published research on it is mostly laboratory-based.
How it works: It absorbs UVB light; its excited state can also cause indirect effects, and researchers have studied this in vitro and in mice.
Risks and caveats: Yeast and cell studies raised photomutagenicity and hormone-receptor questions, while hairless-mouse studies found no carcinogenicity. Labels advise stopping use if rash occurs.
deepLead:
Padimate O (octyl dimethyl PABA, 2-ethylhexyl 4-dimethylaminobenzoate, sold as Escalol 507) is an oily, water-insoluble ester related to PABA that has been used as a UVB filter in sunscreens and lip products . It is approved by one or more agencies including the US FDA, per Wikipedia .
Researchers have debated its photochemistry: in vitro work suggested indirect DNA damage on irradiation, while hairless-mouse studies reported no carcinogenic effect .

name: PABA

angle.text: PABA was one of the first sunscreen actives, used for decades to prevent burning and sun-aged skin, and is now known in appearance culture mainly as the ingredient modern formulas moved away from. Its UVB absorption is well established; long-term appearance trials of PABA are not.

summary: The original UVB sunscreen filter, largely dropped over allergy, staining and phototoxicity concerns.
note: Banned as a sunscreen ingredient in the EU since 2008; can cause contact allergy and photosensitivity.
currentQuick:
PABA was one of the first chemical sunscreen ingredients, patented in 1943. It absorbs UVB light and was widely used in mid-century suncare products.
Its use fell after reports of skin allergy, photosensitivity and clothing stains. The EU banned it as a sunscreen ingredient in 2008, and the US FDA proposed limited allowance in 2019. Derivatives such as padimate O persist in some cosmetics.
How it works: The para-arrangement of its amino and carboxyl groups lets it absorb UVB wavelengths (about 290-320 nm) while passing most UVA.
Risks and caveats: Documented risks include allergic contact dermatitis, photocontact dermatitis and eye irritation. A 1982 study reported sensitisation of cells to near-UV damage. It is banned as a sunscreen filter in the EU.
deepLead:
PABA (para-aminobenzoic acid, 4-aminobenzoic acid) is a small aromatic compound with an amino group and a carboxyl group on opposite sides of a benzene ring. It occurs naturally in foods such as liver, brewer's yeast, mushrooms and whole grains, and is an intermediate in folate synthesis in bacteria, plants and fungi. In appearance culture it is known as one of the first active ingredients used in sunscreens.
As a sunscreen filter, PABA absorbs UVB light (roughly 290 to 320 nm) and lets most UVA pass. It was patented in 1943. Its use declined after reports of allergic contact dermatitis and photocontact dermatitis, staining of clothing, and laboratory studies in the early 1980s suggesting it could sensitise cells to UV damage. The European Union banned it as a sunscreen ingredient in 2008, and in 2019 the US FDA proposed allowing only limited use. Water-insoluble derivatives such as padimate O have continued in some cosmetics.
Evidence for PABA as an appearance product is limited to its historical role as a UVB filter; no current clinical trials of it as a sunscreen appear in the sources reviewed.

name: Cinoxate

angle.text: Cinoxate is an older cinnamate UVB filter, US-approved in 1961, that appeared in some sunscreens to protect skin from sun damage. It is rarely used now and appears mainly in ingredient lists and history; its appearance effect was not studied separately.

summary: An older cinnamate UVB filter, approved in the US in 1961 and now rarely used.
note: Little modern research; only cell-culture and computational safety findings exist.
currentQuick:
Cinoxate is a cinnamate-based UVB filter that the US FDA approved in 1961. It appeared in some older sunscreens.
A 2023 review cited by Wikipedia describes it as no longer commonly used in cosmetics.
How it works: As a cinnamate ester, it absorbs ultraviolet B light in the skin's surface layers.
Risks and caveats: No human safety trials are documented in the sources. A 1989 cell study reported increased chromosome changes when combined with other agents, and a 2024 computational study predicted PPAR-gamma activity.
deepLead:
Cinoxate is an organic UVB filter, an ester of methoxycinnamic acid and 2-ethoxyethanol, used in some sunscreen formulations. According to Wikipedia, the US FDA approved it as a UV filter in 1961, and a 2023 review cited there describes it as no longer commonly used in cosmetic formulations.
Published research on cinoxate is sparse. A 1989 laboratory study found it increased chromosome-level changes in cultured hamster cells exposed to certain damaging agents, and a 2024 computational study flagged it as a possible PPAR-gamma agonist; neither involved human use.

name: Dioxybenzone

angle.text: Dioxybenzone (benzophenone-8) is a sunscreen filter in the US monograph, used to add UVB and short-UVA coverage that protects skin from sun aging. It has almost no dedicated research, so its appearance benefit is inferred from sunscreen-class evidence.

summary: A benzophenone UVB/short-UVA sunscreen filter listed in the US monograph, with almost no dedicated research.
note: Almost all safety data concern other benzophenones, mainly oxybenzone.
currentQuick:
Dioxybenzone (benzophenone-8) is a benzophenone-type UV filter that absorbs UVB and short-wave UVA. It appears in the US sunscreen monograph.
Very little published research addresses it specifically.
How it works: Its benzophenone core absorbs ultraviolet light and dissipates the energy, the same general mechanism as other benzophenone filters.
Risks and caveats: No dioxybenzone-specific human safety data appear in the sources. Studies of benzophenones as a class have looked at environmental presence, coral toxicity and cell-level hormone activity.
deepLead:
Dioxybenzone, also called benzophenone-8, is a benzophenone-derived sunscreen ingredient that absorbs UVB and short-wave UVA light. Chemically it is (2-hydroxy-4-methoxyphenyl)(2-hydroxyphenyl)methanone, a yellow powder that is insoluble in water.
Wikipedia lists it among sunscreen agents approved by one or more agencies without naming which, and gives no safety or history information. Research on benzophenone UV filters as a class, mainly the better-known benzophenone-3 (oxybenzone), has examined environmental occurrence, hormone-related activity in cells and coral toxicity; dioxybenzone itself is rarely the subject of these studies.

name: Sulisobenzone

chain: Less UV damage to skin and hair
angle.text: Sulisobenzone (benzophenone-4) is a water-soluble UV filter in some sunscreens and in hair products meant to protect colour and structure. People use such products for sun protection of skin and dyed hair. Research on it is mostly environmental, not appearance-focused.

summary: A water-soluble benzophenone UV filter (BP-4) used in sunscreens and hair products, studied mostly as an environmental contaminant.
note: Research is mainly environmental, not clinical.
currentQuick:
Sulisobenzone (benzophenone-4) is a UV filter that absorbs UVB and short UVA. Unlike other benzophenones it dissolves in water, so it also appears in some hair products.
Most published work on it concerns its presence in rivers and wastewater rather than human trials.
How it works: It absorbs ultraviolet light through its benzophenone structure; the sulfonic acid group makes it water-soluble.
Risks and caveats: Sources reviewed contain no dedicated human safety trials. Environmental studies report it in surface water, and UV filters as a class have been tested for hormone-like activity in cells and fish.
deepLead:
Sulisobenzone, or benzophenone-4, is a water-soluble benzophenone UV filter that protects against UVB and short-wave UVA light. Its sodium salt is called benzophenone-5. It is used in some sunscreens and, per its cosmetic ingredient listing, in hair products to protect colour and structure.
Wikipedia's entry is a stub covering chemistry and uses only. Research on sulisobenzone is mostly environmental: it has been among the most abundant UV filters detected in Swiss river water, and fish and cell assays have examined hormone-like activity of UV filters. The North American Contact Dermatitis Group has also included UV-filter allergens in its patch-test series.

name: Trolamine salicylate

chain: Mild sun-filter role in old products
angle.text: Trolamine salicylate is best known as the active in odourless muscle-pain creams, and was historically used as a weak UVB absorber in sunscreens and cosmetics. Its appearance link is minor and rarely drawn today; its sunscreen role rests on older formulation use rather than appearance studies.

summary: A weak salicylate UVB filter better known as the active in odourless muscle-pain creams.
note: FDA proposed in 2019 that its sunscreen use is not generally recognised as safe and effective.
currentQuick:
Trolamine salicylate is a salicylate salt best known as the active ingredient in over-the-counter topical pain creams. It has also been used as a weak UVB sunscreen filter.
In 2019 the US FDA proposed that its sunscreen use is not generally recognised as safe and effective.
How it works: The salicylate part absorbs UVB and is described as inhibiting cyclo-oxygenase enzymes locally; triethanolamine neutralises the acid.
Risks and caveats: Labels say external use only. Listed hazards include eye damage and skin or eye irritation. Absorbed salicylate has been measured in blood after topical use in a small human study.
deepLead:
Trolamine salicylate (triethanolamine salicylate) is a salt of triethanolamine and salicylic acid used in over-the-counter topical pain-relief creams such as Aspercreme, and historically as a weak UVB absorber in sunscreens and cosmetics. The salicylate absorbs UVB, the triethanolamine neutralises acidity, and the compound is odourless, unlike menthol-based rubs.
Products are marketed for temporary relief of minor aches in muscles and joints from arthritis, backache, strains and sprains. In 2019 the US FDA proposed classifying its use in sunscreens as not generally recognised as safe and effective. Small trials from the 1980s and 1990s examined its effect on knee osteoarthritis and exercise-induced soreness, with mixed results across studies.

name: Polysilicone-15

chain: Less UV damage to skin and lips
angle.text: Polysilicone-15 (Parsol SLX) is a UVB filter used in EU sunscreens, lip balms and hair products, so users can protect skin, lips and colour-treated hair from sun. Evidence consists of formulation data and case-report safety data, not appearance trials.

summary: A silicone-polymer UVB filter (Parsol SLX) used in sunscreens, lip balms and hair products, with only case-report safety data.
note: Case reports describe contact allergy; no clinical trials found.
currentQuick:
Polysilicone-15 is a large silicone-based UVB filter sold as Parsol SLX. It is used in sunscreens, lip balms and some hair products.
An in vitro study covered it among 18 EU filters, and published safety data are limited to a few case reports.
How it works: It absorbs UVB light with a maximum near 310 nm; its polymer-like size is intended to keep it on the skin's surface.
Risks and caveats: Case reports describe allergic contact dermatitis and cheilitis. No controlled clinical trials are documented.
deepLead:
Polysilicone-15 (dimethicodiethylbenzalmalonate; trade name Parsol SLX, from DSM) is a siloxane-based oligomer used as a UVB filter, with peak absorption near 310 nm. It is a colourless to pale-yellow liquid, practically insoluble in water. It is approved for sunscreens and cosmetics in the EU, and appears in hair products such as shampoos, sprays and colour treatments. It also appears in US-listed lip-balm sunscreens combined with other filters.
An in vitro study of 18 EU-authorised filters examined how filter concentration affects measured SPF. Case reports describe allergic contact reactions to polysilicone-15 in a lip balm and in a sunscreen cream.

name: Tris-biphenyl triazine

chain: Broad UV protection in daily wear
angle.text: Tris-biphenyl triazine (Tinosorb A2B) is a newer particulate filter that skincare enthusiasts look for in daily-wear sunscreens for broad UV coverage against skin aging. Only lab and formulation research exists, with no human trials of its effect on appearance.

summary: Newer particulate UV filter (Tinosorb A2B); only lab and formulation research exists, with no human trials.
note: Approval and permitted concentrations differ by country.
currentQuick:
Tris-biphenyl triazine is a synthetic UV filter sold as Tinosorb A2B. It is a particulate triazine-class filter that absorbs UV and also scatters some light, and it is described as a recent addition to the filters authorised in Europe.
Published work is largely laboratory and formulation research. No clinical trials of its effects on skin appearance were found.
How it works: It absorbs UVB and UVA radiation, and published optical work reports that scattering by its nanoparticles contributes to protection. It has also been tested as a photostabilizer for avobenzone.
Risks and caveats: No compound-specific human safety trials were found. Regulatory approval and maximum concentrations vary by country, and UV filters as a class are the subject of ongoing safety and environmental assessment.
deepLead:
Tris-biphenyl triazine (TBPT), marketed under the trade name Tinosorb A2B, is a synthetic ultraviolet (UV) filter used in sunscreen and daily-wear skincare products. It belongs to the triazine family of filters, which also includes bemotrizinol (Tinosorb S) and phenylene bis-diphenyltriazine .
Published descriptions present it as a relatively recent addition to the small list of UV filters authorised in Europe, and as a particulate (nanoparticle-type) filter that absorbs UV light and also scatters part of it . Wikipedia lists it among UVA- and UVB-protective filters, with approval status and maximum concentrations that differ by jurisdiction .
Published work on the filter consists mainly of formulation, optical and photochemical studies, plus its use as a photostabilizer for other filters such as avobenzone . No clinical trials of its appearance effects were found. In looksmaxxing circles it is discussed only in passing, as one ingredient in sunscreen formulations.

name: Methoxypropylamino cyclohexenylidene ethoxyethylcyanoacetate

angle.text: This L'Oreal filter (Mexoryl 400, UVMune) targets long-wave UVA1, the range tied to wrinkling and pigmentation, and is promoted in La Roche-Posay sunscreens. It gained EU approval in 2019; no published human trials show appearance outcomes.

summary: L'Oreal's UVA1 filter (Mexoryl 400 / UVMune), EU-approved in 2019 with no published human trials.
note: Not recognised by the US FDA; used only in L'Oreal-group products per Wikipedia.
currentQuick:
MCE is a newer organic UV filter that absorbs long-wave UVA (peak 385 nm). L'Oreal markets it as Mexoryl 400, and La Roche-Posay sells it as UVMune.
The EU approved it in 2019 up to 3%, and Australia in 2025. No clinical studies were found.
How it works: It absorbs UVA1 radiation in the 360 to 400 nm range, with its maximum at 385 nm.
Risks and caveats: Public toxicology detail is limited to regulatory concentration limits. The FDA does not currently recognise it for US sunscreens.
deepLead:
Methoxypropylamino cyclohexenylidene ethoxyethylcyanoacetate (abbreviated MCE) is an organic UV filter used in sunscreens to absorb long-wave UVA radiation. According to Wikipedia it was developed by L'Oreal and BASF, and L'Oreal markets it as Mexoryl 400, while its subsidiary La Roche-Posay sells it as UVMune .
It has an absorption maximum at 385 nm, in the UVA1 range (360 to 400 nm) . The EU approved it as a cosmetic UV filter in 2019 at up to 3%, and Australia's Therapeutic Goods Administration followed in 2025 at the same limit; the same page states that the US FDA does not currently recognise it .
No peer-reviewed clinical studies of the filter were found, and public information on its toxicology is limited to regulatory opinions and concentration caps.

name: Phenylene bis-diphenyltriazine

chain: Absorbs UVB, UVA and blue light
angle.text: Phenylene bis-diphenyltriazine (TriAsorB) is a newer filter its developers say covers UV and high-energy blue light, which appeals to users worried about sun-driven pigmentation and aging. The evidence is mostly developer-authored; independent appearance data are not available.

summary: Newer triazine UV filter (TriAsorB) pitched as covering blue light too; evidence is mostly developer-authored.
note: Blue-light claims come mainly from the filter's developers.
currentQuick:
Phenylene bis-diphenyltriazine, sold as TriAsorB, is a newer UV filter that its developers say covers UVB, UVA and blue light.
Published studies are mostly laboratory work plus a small clinical evaluation of blue-light pigmentation, largely from groups linked to its development.
How it works: It is a triazine-class absorber designed to extend sunscreen protection into the high-energy visible (blue) range as well as UV.
Risks and caveats: The EU SCCS published a safety opinion in 2018. No independent long-term human safety trials were found, and approval varies by jurisdiction.
deepLead:
Phenylene bis-diphenyltriazine (PBDT), also known as TriAsorB, is a synthetic UV filter that absorbs UVB and UVA radiation and, according to its developers, also high-energy visible (blue) light . It is a triazine-class filter, listed alongside bemotrizinol and tris-biphenyl triazine in ingredient tables .
Developer-authored papers describe it as a new-generation filter with unusual optical properties and report SPF50+ formulations containing it . The EU Scientific Committee on Consumer Safety published an opinion on its safety (listed under the code S86) .
Human studies are few and come largely from groups associated with its development; they examine blue-light-induced pigmentation and testing methods rather than appearance outcomes over time.

name: Titanium dioxide

chain: Mineral filter reflects and absorbs UV
angle.text: Titanium dioxide is the classic mineral sunscreen filter and white pigment, used in physical sunscreens and tinted SPF to protect skin from sun aging and even out tone for the day. Sunscreen protection is well established; it is weaker on long UVA.

summary: The classic mineral UV filter and white pigment in physical sunscreens and tinted SPF; broad but weaker on UVA I.
note: Inhalation concerns (IARC 2B) apply to dust and sprays; EU banned E171 in food, not in sunscreen.
currentQuick:
Titanium dioxide is a white mineral used as a physical sunscreen filter and a pigment in tinted SPF. Together with zinc oxide it was the only filter the FDA recognised as GRASE as of 2021.
It gives good UVB and UVA II coverage but is weaker in UVA I, and larger particles can leave a white cast.
How it works: It scatters and reflects light and absorbs UV. Nano-sized particles give a sheerer finish.
Risks and caveats: IARC classes inhaled dust as Group 2B and advises against sprayable sunscreens. The EU removed it as a food additive in 2022. Non-nano particles mostly stay in the outer skin layer, though nanoparticle effects on aquatic life are studied.
deepLead:
Titanium dioxide (TiO2), also called titanium white or CI 77891, is a white, water-insoluble mineral compound and the most widely used white pigment. It is found in paints, plastics, paper and toothpaste as well as cosmetics . In skincare it serves as a mineral (physical) UV filter and as a pigment in tinted products.
In sunscreen it is usually paired with zinc oxide. Wikipedia describes mineral filters as working mainly by absorbing UV, with some reflection and scattering, and notes that titanium dioxide gives good protection but does not fully cover the UVA range; zinc oxide has been reported to be superior at 340 to 380 nm . Since 2019 the FDA has sorted UV filters into categories, and as of 2021 only zinc oxide and titanium dioxide were recognised as generally recognised as safe and effective (GRASE) .
Safety discussion centres on nanoparticle forms and on inhalation. The International Agency for Research on Cancer classifies inhaled titanium dioxide dust as Group 2B, possibly carcinogenic to humans, and advises against sprayable sunscreens because of inhalation risk . The EU withdrew authorisation of E171 as a food additive in 2022 after the European Food Safety Authority could not rule out genotoxicity; this does not concern its use in sunscreen .

name: Zinc oxide

chain: Mineral filter blocks UVA and UVB
angle.text: Zinc oxide is a broad-spectrum mineral sunscreen filter used by people seeking gentle, photostable protection that preserves youthful, even skin. It also forms the base of barrier creams. The UV protection is well established; appearance benefit follows from reduced photoaging.

summary: Mineral UV filter and skin protectant with broad UVA/UVB coverage; also the base of diaper-rash and barrier creams.
note: Non-nano forms leave a white cast; nano forms are covered separately.
currentQuick:
Zinc oxide is a mineral powder used as a sunscreen filter and as a skin protectant in diaper-rash and barrier creams. It covers both UVA and UVB and is described as photostable.
As of 2021 it and titanium dioxide were the only FDA-recognised GRASE sunscreen filters. Larger particles leave a white cast.
How it works: It absorbs UV light because of its wide band gap and also scatters some. In skin products it acts as a physical barrier.
Risks and caveats: It is generally described as non-irritating and non-comedogenic. Inhaled fumes can cause metal fume fever, and nano forms are studied for effects on aquatic life.
deepLead:
Zinc oxide (ZnO) is an inorganic white powder used as a mineral UV filter in sunscreens and as a skin protectant in diaper-rash creams, barrier ointments and calamine lotion . Wikipedia calls it the broadest-spectrum UVA and UVB absorber among sunscreen filters and states it is completely photostable .
Zinc compounds have been used in ointments for a very long time; an Indian medical text, the Charaka Samhita, mentions a zinc salve for eyes and wounds . As of 2021 only zinc oxide and titanium dioxide were recognised as generally recognised as safe and effective (GRASE) sunscreen filters by the US FDA; the EU approved zinc oxide as a UV filter in 2016 .
Larger particles produce a white cast, so many modern sunscreens use nanoparticle forms; these are a separate entry on this wiki .

name: Nano zinc oxide

angle.text: Nano zinc oxide is the transparent version of the mineral filter, used so mineral sunscreens go on without a white cast while still protecting skin from sun aging. The sheer finish is directly visible; the debate is about penetration and aquatic toxicity.

summary: Nanoparticle zinc oxide: the invisible-on-skin version of the mineral filter, with debate centred on penetration and aquatic toxicity.
note: EU requires a "nano" label; US does not.
currentQuick:
Nano zinc oxide is zinc oxide in nanometre-sized particles, used so mineral sunscreens look transparent instead of white.
Human studies summarised in reference works report particles staying in the outer skin layer. No studies of appearance outcomes were found.
How it works: It reflects, scatters and absorbs UVA and UVB light; particles are often coated, for example with silica, to limit reactivity.
Risks and caveats: Laboratory studies report cytotoxicity and aquatic toxicity linked to dissolved zinc and reactive oxygen species. The EU requires nano labelling; the US does not.
deepLead:
Nano zinc oxide refers to zinc oxide particles in the nanometre size range, used in sunscreens and other personal-care products as a mineral UV filter. Grokipedia states that the small size permits higher loadings without the white cast of larger particles, and that particles are often silica-coated to limit reactivity on skin .
The question researchers and regulators focus on is whether nanoparticles enter the body through skin. The same page reports negligible dermal penetration in human studies, with particles remaining in the stratum corneum, though some in vitro models suggest minor translocation under extreme conditions; the page carries a caveat about internal inconsistencies in its figures .
In the EU, cosmetic ingredients in nano form must be labelled "nano" under Regulation 1223/2009, and sunscreen use is assessed by the SCCS; US rules do not require nanoparticle labelling . Laboratory studies document antibacterial activity and toxicity to aquatic organisms and cells in culture .

name: Nano titanium dioxide

angle.text: Nano titanium dioxide is used in modern mineral sunscreens so they look sheer rather than chalky, which makes daily wear easier and supports protection against sun aging. Protection is well established for the category; the nano-specific safety debate continues.

summary: Sheer, nanoscale mineral UV filter used in modern sunscreens; protection is well established for the category but the nano-specific safety debate continues.
note: IARC classes inhaled TiO2 dust as possibly carcinogenic; sprays carry inhalation concerns.
currentQuick:
Nano titanium dioxide is a very fine mineral powder used in sunscreens to absorb and scatter UV light. Its small particles make mineral sunscreens look sheerer than older, chalky formulas.
It is often paired with ultrafine zinc oxide. Interest in it comes from people who prefer mineral over organic filters, while its nanoparticle form is also the subject of safety discussion.
How it works: As a wide-bandgap semiconductor it absorbs UV below about 400 nm and scatters little visible light at nanoscale sizes. Under UV it can also generate reactive oxygen species, which is the basis of its photocatalytic uses.
Risks and caveats: IARC classifies inhaled TiO2 dust as Group 2B and advises against sprayable sunscreens. Laboratory studies report gut-barrier and ecological effects at tested exposures. The EU banned it as a food additive in 2022; sunscreen use is regulated separately and no sunscreen-specific clinical trials were found.
deepLead:
Nano titanium dioxide (nano-TiO2) refers to engineered particles of titanium dioxide, typically 1 to 100 nanometres across, that absorb ultraviolet light while remaining largely transparent in visible light. In sunscreens they are used as a mineral UV filter, often alongside ultrafine zinc oxide, to reduce sunburn and long-term sun damage. The smaller particle size is the reason such formulations can look sheer on the skin rather than leaving the opaque white cast associated with older mineral products.
Nanoscale TiO2 also appears in paints, plastics, food colouring, self-cleaning coatings and biomedical research. Its safety has been reviewed for several exposure routes. A 2010 review addressed "nano" titanium dioxide and zinc oxide in sunscreens specifically, and a 2016 review compared toxicity by route of exposure. Regulators have treated inhaled dust and food-additive use differently from topical use.

name: Cerium oxide

angle.text: Cerium oxide is discussed as a possible mineral UV absorber with lower photocatalytic activity than zinc oxide or titanium dioxide, which would suit sunscreens aimed at preventing skin aging. Antioxidant nanoceria research exists; sunscreen evidence for appearance does not.

summary: Industrial ceramic oxide floated as a low-photoreactivity mineral UV absorber; antioxidant nanoceria research exists, sunscreen evidence does not.
note: No human sunscreen studies found; nanoceria safety on skin not established.
currentQuick:
Cerium oxide is a pale powder mostly used to polish glass and in catalysts. It has been suggested as a sunscreen ingredient because it absorbs UV with less photoreactivity than zinc or titanium oxide.
Most of the research is on nanoparticle versions and their antioxidant-like behaviour, not on skin protection in people.
How it works: Ceria flips between Ce3+ and Ce4+ states, which lets nanoparticles mimic antioxidant enzymes in the lab. Its UV absorption comes from the semiconductor-like oxide lattice.
Risks and caveats: No human sunscreen trials were found. Laboratory work shows low cell toxicity in some models, but nanoparticle safety on skin has not been clinically established.
deepLead:
Cerium oxide (cerium(IV) oxide, ceria, CeO2) is a pale yellow-white, water-insoluble ceramic powder with a cubic fluorite crystal structure. It is mainly an industrial material, used for glass polishing, glass decolourising, catalysts including automotive catalytic converters, and fuel cells. In cosmetics discussions it appears as a candidate mineral UV absorber; Wikipedia describes nanoceria as a prospective replacement for zinc oxide and titanium dioxide in sunscreens because of lower photocatalytic activity.
Most of the scientific literature concerns cerium oxide nanoparticles (nanoceria) as redox-active materials that mimic antioxidant enzymes, and their toxicity. No human trials of cerium oxide as a sunscreen or appearance product were found.
